description: We are a group of young, innovative astronomy enthusiasts from Sri Lanka. We would like to present our ideas on how we can educate junior astronauts about interstellar missions. As a team of six individuals, we work together with our combined cognitive power to conquer this competition.
summary: Project eXcalibur is an interactive space education web application designed for learners aged 7 to 12 to experience the thrills of managing a real space mission. Space exploration often oversimplifies the difficulties of keeping an off-world outpost alive. We address this challenge by combining an academy learning hub with a lunar or Martian outpost survival game. Cadets manage their base by adjusting power grids, radiation shields, food production, and oxygen scrubbers. Automated space hazards trigger alarms every 20 seconds, requiring players to balance competing demands under pressure. Incorrect inputs trigger error buzzers and penalties because keeping space potatoes alive is harder than it looks. This project is vital because astronomy is a universally fascinating discipline. By blending formal academic modules on planetary accretion and transit photometry with operational survival gameplay, Project eXcalibur transforms astrophysics into an adventure where education meets entertainment and learning thrives because survival is on the line
details: Project eXcalibur works as an interactive astronomy education platform that guides cadets aged seven to twelve from foundational astrophysics lessons on protoplanetary accretion, frost lines, transit photometry, and habitable zones into a twelve question mastery quiz, a printable flight certificate generator, and a ten Sol Outpost Commander survival simulation. In the simulation, players allocate power across solar arrays, magnetic radiation shields, hydroponics greenhouse scrubbers, and atmospheric life support systems to survive randomized space hazards like solar flares that strike every twenty seconds. The primary benefit of this integrated design is transforming passive textbook reading into active engineering judgment, demonstrating that keeping space crops alive and crew morale intact requires much more focus than simply pressing buttons at random. Our intended impact is to make rigorous space science approachable and exciting for elementary learners, proving that astronomy is an inspiring discipline anyone can master when education is paired with mission survival. We engineered the entire software experience as a single self contained web application using HTML5, Tailwind CSS, vanilla JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas for interactive orbital visualizers, and the Web Audio API for synthesized error buzzers and alarm tones. Our project stands out creatively through high stakes sensory feedback, including red flashing screen alerts, audible mistake buzzers, and mandatory zero percent resets on solar array and food production sliders after every round so players must actively recalibrate their strategy rather than coasting on lucky guesses. Throughout development, our team carefully weighed crucial factors including intuitive visual hierarchy for young readers, balanced difficulty pacing across ten mission cycles, strict input validation, and lightweight browser compatibility so schools and families can launch the mission instantly on standard computers without installing external software.
